newsitem.title: USA: Expert says suicide cult may be copycat of 70s cult.
newsitem.headline: Expert says suicide cult may be copycat of 70s cult.

text.p: The cult whose members took their lives in the belief a UFO would take them to heaven resembles a 1970s cult that disbanded after its hoped-for meeting with aliens never occurred, an expert said on Thursday.

"One theory that seems to be emerging is that it is a spin-off, derivation or a copycat cult of one of the first UFO cults, which was originally called the Bo Peep Cult," said cult expert Jim Siegelman, co-author of the book, "Snapping: America's Epidemic of Sudden Personality Change."

As authorities identified the 39 members of the Heaven's Gate cult and released details of how they took their lives in a million-dollar mansion in affluent Rancho Santa Fe, he said other cult experts increasingly saw parallels to the earlier group.

"The Bo Peep cult was a mobile cult that floated in the Pacific Northwest and West Coast, especially where it believed it was going to rendezvous with extraterrestrials and aliens who were waiting to meet with them," said Siegelman.
Cult experts said some of the names on the postings on the web site of Heaven's Gate, which designed computer Internet web pages, sounded like derivations of Bo and Peep.
"They had names, like Doe and Ti (pronounced Tee), and their affiliation with UFOs indicates there might be some connection or members from the earlier group," said Siegelman.
CBS identified the leader of Heaven's Gate as Marshall Applewhite, who was named by the cult members as "Doe," and was questioned by police as far back as 1974, when a recruiting campaign went sour.
In an aired videotape from 1974, Applewhite spoke of rising from the dead, much as he did in a tape made just days ago and also aired on television broadcasts on Thursday.
The later videotape showed Applewhite telling people he would lead them to "the next level."
"My older member can be your senior shepherd," said Applewhite who appeared in multiple images on the videotape. "You can follow us but you cannot stay here."
A woman, also believed to be a cult member, appears on the tape in an outdoor setting and refers to her meeting with a "King Doe."
"Maybe they're crazy for all I know," she said. "But I don't have any choice but to go for it, because I've been on this planet for 31 years and there's nothing here for me.

"So I don't feel there was any way that anybody could say that I was influenced by somebody's strong personality. The second time I sat with King Doe ... I felt, absolutely ... these people ... there was no lie in them, that there was truth and goodness beyond anything I've ever seen."
Siegelman said he had spoken with several members of the Bo Peep cult through the years.
"We've spoken with people in that group and many were troubled for years afterwards and were not sure of what reality they were in," he said.
Police investigating the deaths of 39 cult members in California confirmed on Thursday the victims died in a mass suicide after eating drug-laced pudding or apple sauce.
Officials said the 21 women and 18 men were between the ages of 20 and 72 and were dressed in black pants, black athletic shoes and black, collarless shirts with large pockets on the front.
Most of the victims were in their 40's and were covered with a purple shroud.
